Chapter 8: Articulating and Communicating Purpose—Practical Tools and Techniques.
You know, having a clear sense of purpose is already powerful. But here’s the thing—when you’re able to actually express and share that purpose with others, its impact grows even stronger.
Whether you’re working on your own, leading a team, or part of a bigger organization, communicating your ‘why’ is what helps build real understanding, trust, and a sense of alignment.
But how do you do it well? It all starts with clarity and authenticity. You don’t need the perfect slogan or some polished mission statement. What really matters is expressing your beliefs in a way that feels honest, and relatable.
One of the best ways to do this is through storytelling. Think about it: when you share a real-life example that shows your purpose in action, people can see what you stand for and why it matters.
Here’s a simple framework you can use:
First, start with why. Explain the core belief, or that deeper motivation, behind what you do.
Then, show how. Describe the values, principles, or the methods that guide your approach.
And finally, end with what. Share the tangible results or outcomes that naturally flow from your purpose.
For example, imagine a nonprofit leader saying, “We believe that every child deserves a safe and nurturing environment.” That’s their why.
Next, they explain how: “We work closely with families and communities to provide support and resources.”
And finally, the what: “As a result, more children are able to thrive and reach their potential.”
Storytelling like this really works, because it speaks to both the heart and the mind. When you share a personal story or a customer’s journey, you invite others to see themselves in that experience—and suddenly, your purpose feels real and personal to them, too.
There are a few other practical techniques to keep in mind:
Use simple, conversational language. Skip the jargon and buzzwords—just speak like you would to a friend.
Be consistent. Repeat your key messages often, across different settings and audiences.
And don’t forget to invite feedback and start a dialogue. That way, you’ll know if your purpose is really resonating and being understood.
Sometimes, visual tools can make your purpose even more tangible. Picture a tree: the roots are your core beliefs, the trunk stands for your values and methods, and the branches and leaves represent the outcomes you’re striving for.
The real goal here isn’t to persuade or impress anyone. It’s about inviting others into a shared journey. When people truly get your purpose—and believe in it—they’re much more likely to support you, bring their own ideas, and even become advocates for your cause.
And remember, communicating purpose isn’t a one-time thing. It’s an ongoing practice. As you grow and change, keep refining your message, listen to feedback, and look for new ways to bring your ‘why’ to life.
